RAJYA SABHA [19 December, 2002] 
SHRIV. V. RAGHAVAN: Hon. Chairman, Sir. the hon. Minister in his 
reply has stated that MTNL in Delhi and Mumbai have had private agencies to 
collect the outstanding dues for the Dolphin sen/ices. Is it a first step to privatise 
the public sector unit while the MTNL itself takes steps against the defaulters? 
SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN: Sir, as far as MTNL's privatisation is 
concerned, this is neither first step nor last step. As I said, last time, last week 
on the same day, Government has no proposal to privatise MTNL or to disinvest 
beyond what is already disinvested in MTNL. As far as hiring the private agency 
is concerned, Sir, hon. Member must be concerned, and I am also concerned 
that against the bills which were submitted to the customers, the MTNL's 
normal system could not recover the dues from the customers and a large 
number of defaulters are there. So, hiring some agency to get money from 
defaulters, in no way, can be construed as privatisation. So, I again assure the 
hon. Members that, in the near future, we have no proposal for privatisation of 
MTNL. 
SHRI V. V. RAGHAVAN: Sir, may I know from the hon. Minister the 
latest position in regard to providing WLL services throughout the country, and 
on what ground private operators are opposing this move? 
SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN: I will require a separate notice for that 
because this question, if you look at it, only talks about MTNL's dues from 
the Dolphin area—Cellular. So, at this juncture, it is difficult for me to answer this 
question. If a separate notice on WLL comes, I will come with preparation and 
happily answer. 
SHRI N. K. PREMACHANDRAN: Sir, the Cellular service, which has 
been started by the BSNL, got a good response in the State of Kerala and the 
demand is very huge. But, the SIM cards and units are not available. We have 
read in the newspapers that private companies are behind the artificial shortage 
of SIM cards. A huge response has come from consumers, especially a very 
good response has come from the State of Kerala. Has it come to the notice of 
the hon. Minister why such shortage is there? 
SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN: Mr. Chairman, if you again permit me, I 
will try to answer this question in a general way because the question put up 
to me is,  
 
 
 
2 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 [19 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
consumers default. So, it has nothing to do with the BSNL Cellular service. At 
present, I am not prepared. But 1 can assure you that BSNL is not helping 
private operators by shortage of SIM cards. The BSNL has just started. If I 
would have to help private operators, I would not have entered into the market. 
Nobody forced BSNL to go into the market. So, when we entered into the 
market, we would like to dominate the market. We would like about 4 million 
customers in a year's time or so. The response to the BSNL's Cellular service—
Cell-one -is very good. But, there are teething problems in the beginning. So, 
shortage of SIM cards in Kerala or elsewhere in the country, in no way, should be 
treated as a proof of helping private operators. If I have to help private operators, I 
would not have entered into the business. So, we have entered into business and 
we would like to take a substantial share in a competitive environment. 
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: Mr. Chairman, the hon. Minister has 
replied that in order to collect the outstanding dues certain private agencies will be 
engaged. Sir, there is already a machinery set up in the MTNL to collect dues. 
Sir, the default has occurred just because of certain technical snags, as pointed out 
by the Minister. Therefore, if those technical snags are being removed, and if the 
same machinery is being utilised, you can collect the dues from the defaulters 
with the help of this machinery. Therefore, instead of engaging some other 
agency, why can't you think of that? 
SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN: Sir. this is a suggestion for action. But, as I 
said earlier, one must understand that we should not be very touchy about 
deploying private agencies to collect our own dues. What is wrong in it? We 
want to collect our dues, and the MTNL's normal machinery is not used to do 
this thing. It is true that the software problem was a part of it. But the collection 
problem is also a part of it. So, we are trying to tackle both the problems, and as 
I said, hiring any private agency for security purpose, and hiring any private 
agency for billing purpose, should not be treated as privatisation, and as I 
assured, there is no question of privatisation. I think, this should be allowed, 
as lonq as MTNL gets its dues from the defaulting customers.

SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): Sir, my first 
supplementary is regarding (c) part of my question.The existing procedure 
 
4

[19 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
for securing administrative approval and issuance of technical and financial 
sanction takes as much as 8 months, leaving hardly 3-4 months for execution 
of road development works. To cut short this time lag, is it not feasible and 
desirable to delegate the powers of approval to an expert State level 
Committee, with proper Central representation? 
MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B. C. KHANDURl: Sir, the first part of the hon. 
Member's question that it takes 8 months to get the approval, is not correct. I 
have got with me details right from the beginning, that is, November, 2000, 
when the scheme started, and the first proposal from Rajasthan came in 
December, 2000. From December, 2000 till now, I have got all the details, and 
without going into the details, let me say that it has taken initially 3 weeks to 4 
weeks. At the most, we have taken 8 weeks. So, his query that it has taken 
more than 8 months, is not correct. We have never taken that much time, and it is 
not going to be that much duration. On an average, it will not be more than 4 to 6 
weeks. Now, as regards having an expert committee, in my opinion, that is 
going to take more time. I would like to inform the House about the time that 
we take. The procedure is very simple. The State Government sends us a list. 
We only want to make sure that, first of all, it is as per the criteria laid down by 
us. Secondly, works are being distributed in the entire State. We have cases 
where a large number of proposals came for a particular constitutency of an 
MLA or an MP. Therefore, we have now decided to have a map for each State, 
and in that, we plan them accordingly, and our effort is to see that it is evenly 
distributed all over the country. Therefore, I think, the present system is 
working well. 
SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): Sir, I would like to 
draw the attention of the House to one thing. The Ministry of Road Transport 
and Highways issued guidelines for the implementation of the scheme on 13th 
October, 2000, which were subsequently amended on 13th December, 
20OO.The guidelines were further amended on 13th July. Sir, amendment itself is 
taking more than 6 to 7 months. So, to say that it has taken 6 weeks' time, is not

So, what the hon. Minister has said, is not absolutely correct. But, nonetheless, my 
second supplementary is, in view of the strategic importance of Rajasthan, 
being the largest. State on the border, and strategically and geologically situated, 
between the capital and the trade and industrial centres in the South, does the

Government propose to relax the limitation on the accumulation and 
utilisation of funds on year to year basis? If so, I want to know the details in this 
regard. 
MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B. C. KHANDURI: Sir, let me clarify the first 
point about the guidelines. Before December, 2000, when the... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: There is no need to make any clarification. 
MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B. C. KHANDURI: No. Sir. he has made an 
observation which needs clarification from the Ministry's side. Before 13th 
December, 2000, there existed a system of CRF, which was changed and 
revamped by the Parliament and enacted in December, 2000. As against the. 
earlier CRF, the changed system is a comprehensive one. The earlier system 
was based on a CRF, system through which we were collecting about Rs. 25 
crores; now, we are collecting Rs. 6000 crores. Therefore, there is a 
difference. But after 13th July, 2001 we have not made any further changes. 
As regards giving additional allocation to Rajasthan, there is a system by 
which CRF is allocated; 60 per cent, based on the consumption of diesel and 
petrol, and 40 per cent based on the geographical area. And therefore, every 
State gets an allocation; Rajasthan is getting about Rs. 75 crores. Secondly, year 
by year allocation is an. irrelevant thing, because this is a non-lapsabie amount; 
whatever amount is unspent this year, goes into the next year. 
DR. L. M. SINGHVI: Sir, for the States which are difficult to access, and 
areas where there are no other adequate means of transport, such as Rajasthan, is 
there a proposal for consideration for some additional funds, particularly, in view of 
the fact that now, Rajasthan is suffering from drought? Labour intensive schemes 
would be extremely helpful to the suffering people. 
MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B. C. KHANDURI: As regards the idea that 
certain States don't have other means of communication, we understand this 
requirement. But, at the moment, there is a norm. We have tried to 
accommodate some other States—of course, Rajasthan does not fit into that 
category—such as the North-Eastern States or the hilly areas, where apart from 
road, there is no mode of transportation. We are trying to give them additional 
allocation, not in terms of money, but in terms of sanctions. Normally, we sanction 
twice the amount of allocation, but in their case, we have sanctioned thrice the 
amount of allocation. Thus, we have tried

TION AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) wether it is a fact that Government have changed the clauses of the

THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN ): (a) to (c) A Statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
 
7

RAJYA SABHA [19 December, 2002] 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Licenses for Cellular Mobile Telephone Service (CMTS) have 
been granted to private operators as a result of tenders received in three phases in 
the year 1992,1995 and 2001. Amendment to the clauses of the License 
Agreement have been carried out from time to time as per the emerging 
requirements. Salient features of the amendments carried out so far are given in 
the Statement-I {See below). 
(c) These amendments to License Agreements have been uniformly applied 
to all the Licenses and therefore, all th e Licensees are beneficiaries; list of 
Licensees indicating the Service Area of each Licensee is at Statement-ll. 
Statement-l 
Salient Features of the Amendments to License Agreement 
(i) By an amendment dated 23.10.1997 transfer or assignment of License 
in accordance with conditions of Tripartite Agreement amongst 
Licensor, Licensee and Lenders,was permitted. This was to facilitate 
financing of projects by the Lenders. 
(ii) By an amendment dated 23.10.1997, the limit on external/ 
international commercial borrowing imposed in the Licence was 
modified to be in accordance with the guidelines issued on the subject 
from time to time by Ministry of Finance, Government of India. 
(ill) By an offer of Migration Package made in July, 1999, the existing 
Licensees were migrated from fixed license fee regime to the revenue 
sharing arrangement under New Telecom Policy, 1999. The main 
features of this Migration are as below: 
(a) The licence period was extended from 10 years to 20 years. 
(b) Change from duopoly to multipoly regime with effect from 
1.8.1999 i.e. the Licensees surrendered their right to operate 
in a duopoly regime (of only two private operators) with the 
condition that any number of additional private 
 operators can be inducted. 
 
8

[19 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(c) Change from fixed licence fee as committed at the time of 
grant of licences to licence fee as percentage of revenue 
earned. The licence fee at present for category 'A' . 'B' and 'C 
Service Areas is 12%, 10% and 8% of "Adjusted Gross 
Revenue' respectively, inclusive of Universal Service 
Obligation (USO), apart from separate charges for use of 
Wireless Frequency Spectrum. 
(d) Migration Package is deemed as a full and final settlement 
of all disputes whatsoever, upto the cut off date of migration 
irrespective of whether they are related with the Migration 
Package or not. 
(iv) By an Order dated 1.10.1999 the Cellular License was made 
technology-neutral; earlier to this it was mandatory for the 
Licensees to use Global System of Mobile Communications 
(GSM) technology. 
(v) By an amendment dated 25.09.2001 transfer or assignment of 
licence was permitted in the situation of merger of licensee 
companies if approved by a High Court so long as competition is not 
compromised. 
(vi) By an order dated 1.2.2002 allocation of additional specturm 
beyond 6.2 MHz on payment of additional spectrum charges, 
subject to availability of the spectrum and justification, was 
permitted.

3007. SHRI NANDl YELLAIAH: W ill the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have to shell out extra $ 450 million to import 
more edible oil this year to compensate the shortfall in oil seeds production; 
(b) if so, whether Government had to spend $ 2,500 million on import of 
edible oil between October, 2001 and September, 2002 against usual a nnual 
import bill of $ 2,000 million; 
(c) if so, the reasons for the shortfall in edible oil production; and 
(d) the steps being taken to improve the production of edible oil in the 
country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. SREENIVASA 
PRASAD): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) Some of the reasons for the shortfall in edible oils are:— 
81 

RAJYA  SABHA [19 December, 2002] 
(i) Crushing of oilseeds namely. Mustard/rapeseed, Groundnut and 
Sesame is reserved under Small Scale Sector and Oilseed Growers' 
Co-operatives.The capacity utilization generally ranges from an average 
of 10% for the ghanis (small-scale sector) to around 30% in case of 
the expellers in the organized sector. 
(11) Unrestricted growth in the industry consequent upon de-licensing of the 
vegetable oil industry. 
(ill) Creation of capacity totally incommensurate with availability of raw 
materials. 
(iv) Obsolete Technology. 
(v) Very low margin because of s tiff competition, inefficiency of 
operations etc. 
(vi) Speculative nature of trade. 
(vii) Mismatch between (low) raw material production and (high) 
processing capacity leading to a situation of too much capacity 
chasing too few raw materials (oilseeds). 
(vlii) Fragmentation of capacities, poor scale economies, large idle 
capacity. 
(ix) High cost of raw material and processing renders products like edible 
and other oils uncompetitive and affects export prospects. 
(x) Low priced imported oils eat into already fragile trade margins on 
domestic oils. 
(xl) No wonder, the processing industry especially oil milling and 
solvent extraction suffers from pervasive sickness, 
(d) The remedial measures taken and efforts made to increase the 
indigenous production of oilseeds and of edible oils include;- 
(i) A Centrally Sponsored Oilseeds Production Programme is 
implemented in 25 States covering 395 selected Districts to increase 
the production of oilseeds edible oils in the country. 
(ii) A Technology Mission on Oilseeds is in place Jo harness appropriate 
production, processing and management technology. 
82 

[19 December. 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(iii) Intensification of research effo rts to increase the production of 
oilseeds. 
(iv) Increasing the areas under non-traditional oilseeds crops, like 
soyabean and sunflower and exploitation of oilseeds of tree and forest 
origin, rice bran etc. 
(v) Setting up of necessary processing and infrastructural facilities to 
keep pace with the production programme of oilseeds. 
(vi) Assistance for oil palm development. 
(vii) Better incentives to producers through fixation of Minimum Support Price 
(MSP) of major oilseeds. 
(viii) Use of indigenous oils in the manufacture of Vanaspati to at least 
25% of the production on a monthly basis is mandatory at present. 
Higher use of expeller mustard oil in the manufacture of Vanaspati upto 
30% has also been allowed. The objective is to incentivise the 
farmers in terms of better returns for their production. 
In order to harmonise the interests of domestic oilseeds growers, 
consumers and processors and to regulate imports of edible oils to the extent 
possible, the duty structure on edible oils is reviewed from time to time.

(a) whether it is a fact that regular training is being provided In 
countries adjoining India to terrorists in carrying out their terrorist activities 
against India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the action Government propose to take against such countries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) to (c) 
Palfistan 
Pakistan has established an elaborate infrastructure for the recruitment; 
indoctrination and training of terrorists on its territories and territories under its 
control, to support its policy of sponsoring cross border terrorism in Jammu & 
Kashmir and other parts of India. Information 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
105 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December, 2002] 
regarding terrorist infrastructure, in  Pakistan and Pakistan controlled 
territories, for support to terrorism is appropriately shared with other 
countries as a part of the global efforts against international terrorism. 
Government are determined and firmly committed to fight terrorism by all 
means until it is decisively crushed. 
Bangladesh 
The Government of India Is aware of the reports that agencies, inimical 
to India's interests, including the ISI, are misusing the territory of Bangladesh 
for their anti-India activities. 
The Government of India has been regularly taking up these security-related 
issues with Bangladesh at different levels through diplomatic channels and 
institutional mechanism existing between the two countries. The Government of 
Bangladesh has assured that it would not allow its territory to be used for 
activities inimical to India's interests. The Bangladesh foreign minister during 
his visit to India on 16-17 June, 2002 has informed of the decision taken at the 
highest level in the Government not to allow presence of Indian insurgents or 
their free movement across the border. 
Myanmar 
The Government is aware of reports that groups and organizations inimical 
to India's interests are misusing the territory of Myanmar for their activities. 
Most of groups are linked to members of North-East insurgent groups. 
There are institutionalized mechanism where two countries interact 
regularly to address issues related to border management. 
Nepal 
Government is concerned about ISI misusing the Nepalese territories and the 
open India-Nepal border for activities inimical to India's interests and is seized 
of the matter. 
There is close cooperation between Nepal and India on the issue of cross 
border terrorism. Both Governments have agreed that they would 
106 

[19 December. 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
not allow their territories to be used for activities inimical to each other. A 
bilateral institutional mechanism has also been evolved which includes a joint 
working group on border management and Home Secretary level talks. The 
special service bureau has been deployed along the border with Nepal to 
strengthen security in the border areas. The extradition arrangements between 
India and Nepal are presently governed by the Treaty of Extradition of 
1953.The Government of India has proposed that the Treaty be updated and has 
handed over to His Majesty's Government of Nepal (HMGN) a model text of an 
updated Extradition Treaty. 
Bhutan 
The presence of ULFA, NDFB and KLO militants on Bhutanese 
territory has been a subject of discussion with the Government of Bhutan. The 
National Assembly of Bhutan adopted a series of Resolutions in 1999, 2000 
and again in 2001 to control this menace. The extradition arrangements 
between India and Bhutan are governed by the Extradition Agreement signed 
between the two countries on May 20, 1997. Under this Agreement, India and 
Bhutan are committed to safeguarding each other's security and stability.

on the recommendations of the Expert Group on Estimation of Proportion 
and Number of Poor (Lakdawala Committee), uses State-specific poverty

expenditure of Rs.327.56 in rural areas and Rs.454.11 in urban areas.

prices of commodities in different States, the poverty lines differ from State 
to State.

Pradesh with Rs. 262.94 per person per month and highest in Kerala with Rs. 
374.79 per person per month; in urban areas, the poverty line is lowest in 
Assam with Rs. 343.99 per person per month and highest in Maharashtra 
with Rs. 539.71 per person per month.

Criteria for the declaration of new National Higfjway 
(i) Roads which run through the lengh and breadth of the country.

connecting mutually the State capitals.

centres.

(vi) Arterial roads which enable sizeable reduction in travel distance and

Now, I raise this question for the reason that the Issue of probity in 
public life has to be independently considered. The first Issue, which this 
House must be concerned with, is that the effect of this law is to substantially 
set aside the effect of the judgment of the Supreme Court and the effect of the 
order of the Election Commission. Besides being impracticable in many 
manners, both the judgment of the Supreme Court and the order of the 
Election Commission, have taken away the legislative jurisdiction of the 
Parliament, and decided that now a part of the legislative jurisdiction goes to 
the Supreme Court by this judicial pov^rer and a part of the legislative 
jurisdiction gets further added on to the authority of the Election Commission, 
and it may be saying that, "Well, now I will have the power to decide on this". 
What is the effect of this? Section 36 of the Representation of the People Act 
may give 4-5 reasons on the basis of which a nomination can be rejected. 
Read jointly, the effect of the Supreme Court judgment and the Election 
Commission; they have added five more reasons why a nomination can be 
rejected, and some of those reasons give absolutely arbitrary power which -- 
as I said on the basis of the experiences of one of our neighbouring countries -- 
could be effectively used in a given situation to subvert the very institution of 
elections. We have seen that happening in our neightxjuring country, and this 
is something which we must be very careful about; and one of the reasons. I 
believe, why this legislation must be passed is that this encroachment on 
parliamentary jurisdiction by any other authority, however high it may be, has to 
come to an end. This cannot be permitted to continue. If it does continue, it 
brings about an imbalance in the entire functioning of our democracy where 
separation of powers between the Legislatur e and the Judiciary is a part of the 
basic structure and is an inherent component of our democracy. 
Secondly. Madam, as far as the main issue is concerned, the concern 
really has been on issues of criminals entering public life, how do we stop that. 
That is an issue which the Parliament has to now consider how to address. We 
have had several all-party meetings. There have been suggestions of the Law 
Commission; there have been suggestions of the Election Commission that the 
framing of the charge should be considered as sufficient to prevent a person 
from contesting elections. Whenever all-party meetings have been held, except 
for one party from the State of Sikkim,

Why don't I consider this Bill good enough? During the last several 
years, we have been trying to introduce reforms in the electoral system in a 
piecemeal manner. We don't realise the simple fact that the electoral system, 
which is the core of the parliamentary democracy, is an integrated system. If 
we handle a problem without handling the related problems, it is as good as 
not handling that problem effectively. The piecemeal approach, which had 
been followed during the last 30 years of electoral reforms in our country, has 
landed us in a situation where the whole system has become discredited in the 
eyes of the people and we ourselves realise it. 
A mention has been made by Shri Bhardwaj about the need for a 
comprehensive approach to electoral reforms. It should not mean a committee 
again. So many committees have gone into the electoral reforms issue, 
starting from the Jagannath Rao Committee, the Tarkunde Committee, the 
V.R. Krishna Iyer Committee, the Indrajit Gupta Committee, the 
Venkatachaliah Commission, the Law Commission and the Election 
Commission. We have any number, of good recommendations and 
suggestions emanating from various Committees and Commissions. All that is 
needed is. the will to implement them. If somebody sits down and tries to 
tackle the problem in an integrated, comprehensive manner, a draft Bill can be 
brought before the Parliament any time. 
One argument that has been raised against a comprehensive 
legislation for electoral reforms--l read about this point in certain articles and 
speeches-is that no other advanced democracy has a comprehensive 
legislation covering all aspects of the electoral system or parliamentary 
system. One or two western countries have attempted a few reforms partly, but 
no comprehensive electoral reforms have been attempted. But my point is that 
India, unfortunately, is not in a situation as that of the advanced democracies, 
Our system has failed. Our electoral system has brought us more discredit 
than credit during the last several years. It has been brought out by the Chief 
Election Commission that the Eleventh Lok Sabha had 40 MPs with a criminal 
background. Some people may justify it by saying that they are technical 
offences or they are not serious enough to be called criminal offences. But the 
fact is that 700 MLAs -- I am referring  to that period -- and 40 MPs -- I am 
referring to the Eleventh Lok Sabha --had criminal background. If you say that 
the western countries are not having it. therefore, we cannot go in for it in the 
east, maybe, it is only evading the issue.

May I make some suggestions for the consideration of the hon. 
Minister, through you, Sir? You may take note of the following seven points 
which I am going to make and try to bring a Bill. In my view, if you adopt all 
these seven points, it may satisfy all sections of the people. 
First, defection should instantly result in disqualification, This subject 
has been discussed threadbare in our country and the inevitable last step that 
we have to take is, as I said just now, instant disqualification. Second, there 
has to be a statutory limit of 10 per cent of the strength of the Lower House for 
the size of the Ministry. We try to fight corruption but we forget that defection 
and corruption arise largely because of the anxiety, greed or ambition, 
undisclosed in many cases, of MLAs and legislators. Once they are elected to 
a legislature, they have also the right to sit on the Treasury Benches or to 
become Ministers. Third, no legislator should be appointed - though In the 
States, it has become a common practice - as Chairman of any corporation or 
public sector undertaking, A lot of corruption takes place and a lot of 
malpractice takes place because we accommodate certain people, who cannot 
be accommodated in the Ministry, through chairmanship of corporations or 
public sector undertakings. 
Fourth, if you have a coalition government, there has to be a 
prescribed minimum strength for a coalition partner to have a seat in that 
Government. You can be a member of the coalition or the group, but to 
become a Minister there has to be a minimum number of members in the party. 
There are States in India where a one-member party or a two-member party 
has representation in the Council of Mincters. This has created a vested 
interest in party splitting because to be small in number has become 
advantageous as they get ministership or other positions. Fifth, no political 
party, which does not publish its audited accounts for the knowledge of the 
people, for the information of the f:30ple, should be allowed as a registered 
party. The allocation of symbol is only for registered parties. Every one has to 
submit himself, every party has to submit itself to this bare necessity of having 
to publish audited accounts; the statement of income and expenditure. These 
are the main holes where corruption takes place. I am not talking of the small 
loopholes. We have to plug the big holes. Sixth, affidavit should be filed about 
the assets and liabilities, not merely by the person who has been elected but 
every candidate should be asked to do that.
